options: A structured walkthrough of a hypothetical incident scenario with the real IR team, without touching any real systems
A live simulated attack run against production systems without warning anyone
A written exam the IR team takes individually with no discussion
A one-time certification test required only for new hires
questions.explain: It's a rehearsal of the plan, playbooks, and roles against a scenario, with nothing real actually touched or broken.

questions.q: What is an "inject" in a tabletop exercise?
options: A new piece of information the facilitator introduces mid-exercise to evolve the scenario
A real malware sample deployed onto a test server
The final score given to the team at the end of the session
A legal document signed before the exercise can begin
questions.explain: Injects force the team to apply the plan and playbooks to developments nobody had time to prepare for in advance.

questions.q: In the Friday-ransomware tabletop example, what did the backup-related inject reveal?
options: The most recent backup job had actually failed silently eleven days earlier, and nobody had noticed
The backups were perfectly fine and required no further action
There were no backups configured for that server at any point
The backup job succeeded but took much longer than expected
questions.explain: A gap like a silently failed backup only surfaces when someone actually checks it during the exercise.

questions.q: Why would the RACI gap in the tabletop example -- two people both believing they're Accountable for approving contact with a negotiator -- likely go undiscovered without running the exercise?
options: It only becomes visible when two people both actually reach for the same decision at the same time, which re-reading a document on paper doesn't reveal
RACI gaps are always obvious just from looking at an org chart
The gap would have been caught automatically by the severity classification system
RACI gaps only matter after an incident is already fully resolved
questions.explain: Gaps like this surface only when a real team tries to actually use the plan against a moving scenario.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real value a tabletop exercise delivers, beyond satisfying a compliance checkbox?
options: Finding gaps in the plan and playbooks while there's time to fix them, and building the team's muscle memory in their own roles, at a far lower cost than learning the same gaps during a real incident
Guaranteeing that no real incident will ever happen again
Replacing the need for a written incident response plan entirely
Providing the IR team with a day off from their regular duties
questions.explain: The gaps found and the familiarity built are the real payoff -- the compliance requirement some frameworks impose is secondary to that.
